summary: For ages 13–14: build the distinction between rational and irrational numbers from the decimal signature (terminating OR repeating = rational; non-terminating AND non-repeating = irrational) and develop the idea of density — that infinitely many numbers lie between any two distinct numbers. The guidance aims to counter the 'infinite decimal = irrational' and 'discrete line' misconceptions, and to keep irrationals (√2, π) in their exact symbolic form while locating them approximately on a number line.
misconceptions: Believing any number with infinitely many decimals is irrational (0.333… is rational)
Thinking √2 or π 'equal' their rounded decimals (1.414, 3.14)
Assuming there is a 'next' number after a given one, or a smallest gap on the line
Confusing 'irrational' with 'very large' or 'undefined' rather than non-repeating-non-terminating
Thinking there are finitely many numbers between two close decimals like 0.12 and 0.13

activities.title: Decimal-signature classifier: repetition, not length, decides
steps: For each, write out or stream the decimal expansion and decide whether it TERMINATES or REPEATS. For √2 and π, note that a finite list of digits can never show that a decimal does NEITHER: some rationals have very long repeating blocks (1/97 repeats only after 96 digits). We know √2 and π are irrational because it has been proved, so their decimals never terminate or repeat.
Mark the repeating block when there is one (e.g. box the 3 in 0.3̅, or the 142857 in 1/7) and write the equivalent fraction.
State a rule in your own words for deciding rational vs irrational, then test it against √9 = 3 and 0.333…
Keep √2 and π written exactly as symbols, noting that 1.414… and 3.14… are only approximations.
Locate √2 and π approximately on a number line (e.g. √2 just past 1.4, between 1 and 2; π between 3 and 4) using their decimal approximations, while keeping the exact symbol pinned alongside.
activities.insight: A number is rational exactly when it can be written as a ratio of two integers — which shows up as a terminating OR repeating decimal. The deciding feature is whether the digits settle into a repeat, not how many digits there are: 0.333… is endless yet rational (=1/3). √2 is proved to be irrational, so its expansion never repeats. Checking a finite number of digits could never establish that on its own.

activities.title: Squeeze another number in: density of the line
steps: Name two close numbers, e.g. 0.12 and 0.13 (or 1/4 and 1/3).
Find a number strictly between them — averaging the two is one reliable method (e.g. 0.125).
Now find a number between THAT one and the upper end, and again, and again.
Argue why this process can never run out, and conclude how many numbers lie between the original pair.
Explain why there is no 'next' number after a given one, unlike the integers.
activities.insight: Between any two distinct numbers there are infinitely many others, so the number line is dense: there is no smallest gap and no 'next' number. This contrasts with the discrete, consecutive structure of the integers.

activities.title: Dialogue: why √2 cannot be a fraction
steps: Work through the classic argument: suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms, and reason about whether a and b can both be chosen with no common factor.
Respond to Socratic prompts about what would have to be true of a² and b², and where a contradiction arises.
Then tackle the intuition probe: 'Is there a number right after 0.12?' and explain your answer.

Try to write π as a fraction of two whole numbers (e.g. 22/7 or 355/113) and check that these are only approximations. Note that mathematicians have proved π is irrational, though the proof is beyond this level, which is why its decimal never terminates or repeats.
activities.insight: Some numbers genuinely cannot be written as a ratio of integers — this is a provable fact, not just 'it has lots of decimals'. Engaging with the proof-by-contradiction and the 'no next number' question deepens understanding of what irrationality and density actually mean.

activities.title: Reference anchor: nested number sets
steps: Study a nested-sets diagram: integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals filling the gaps in the reals.
For each region, note example numbers and their decimal signature (terminating / repeating / non-repeating).
Place given numbers into the correct region and justify the placement by the rational/irrational test.
activities.insight: The number systems nest: every integer is rational, every rational is real, and irrationals occupy the reals that are not rational. This gives a map for where any number sits.

activities.title: Consolidation: sort and justify
steps: Sort a mixed set (e.g. 0.333…, √2, 3/8, 0.25, √9, π) into rational vs irrational.
Choose which of a list is irrational and explain the reason, not just the choice (e.g. 'which is irrational: 0.333…, √2, 3/8, 0.25?').
Given a repeating decimal, write the equivalent fraction.
For a classification you make, state the decision rule you applied.
activities.insight: Once the concepts are built, fluent classification and fraction-recovery confirm that the learner applies the repetition/ratio test rather than surface cues.

checkQuestion: Is 0.333... (the 3 repeating forever) rational or irrational? And how many numbers are there between 1/4 and 1/3? Explain both.
checkAnswer: 0.333... is rational — it equals 1/3, a ratio of two integers, and a repeating decimal is always rational. There are infinitely many numbers between 1/4 and 1/3 (indeed between any two distinct numbers).
